r0.why: Scratch resistance, 1 to 10, harder scratches softer [1]; natural sample visibly scratching another [6]; Mohs 1812 [2].

r1.why: Antiquity, Theophrastus c. 300 BC and Pliny [4]; diamond hardest known then, top arbitrarily 10 [9].

r2.why: Reference minerals widespread in rocks [15], measuring method [10], apatite/fluorite example giving 4 to 5 [11].

r3.why: Technical meaning of scratching [12], microscopic dislocations from lower materials [13], permanent but not counted [14].

r4.why: Qualitative ordinal [1][16], corundum/topaz/diamond absolute hardness ratios [17], one of several definitions, some more quantitative [3].

r5.why: Non-minerals assigned hardness [21], mixtures problem [22], granite 6 to 7 [23], topaz-rich granite composition values [24].

r6.why: Imprecise but used by field geologists with scratch kits [25], poor industrial predictor [5], milling [27][28], electronics testing [29].
